passage: A soap film stretches across a wire rectangle. A loose thread rests inside the film as a closed loop. When the film inside the loop is removed, the remaining film pulls the thread outward. The thread becomes round because the pull acts around its edge. Here, the loop means the thread, not the wire frame.

A soap film stretches across a wire rectangle. A loose thread rests inside the film as a closed loop. When the film inside the loop is removed, the remaining film pulls the thread outward. It becomes round because the remaining film pulls around the edge of the thread. Here, the loop means the thread, not the wire frame.

Jon watches a narrow beam reflected by a small mirror onto a screen. The mirror and screen have separate stands. Jon turns the mirror while Mae keeps the screen still. The bright spot moves across the screen. Their notes must identify which object turned, since moving the spot does not mean that its supporting screen moved.

Jon watches a narrow beam reflected by a small mirror onto a screen. The mirror and screen have separate stands. Mae turns the mirror while Jon keeps the screen still. The bright spot moves across the screen. Their notes must identify which object turned, since moving the spot does not mean that its supporting screen moved.

Two classroom sound makers use stretched strips of rubber. One strip is wide, and the other is narrow. Their lengths and the distances between their supports are equal. A student plucks each strip once and records how quickly its motion repeats. Before comparing the records, the student checks that both strips were pulled equally tight. Width is the planned difference in this comparison. A difference in tension would introduce a second possible reason for different motion, even though both sounds were recorded by the same microphone.

Two classroom sound makers use stretched strips of rubber. One strip is wide, and the other is narrow. Their lengths and the distances between their supports are equal. A student plucks each strip once and records how quickly its motion repeats. Before comparing the records, the student checks that both strips were pulled equally tight and that the room temperature stayed the same. Width is the planned difference in this comparison. A difference in tension would introduce a second possible reason for different motion, even though both sounds were recorded by the same microphone.

A bicycle wheel turns freely on a classroom stand. A small patch of bright tape marks one place on its rim. A complete turn means that the patch returns to its starting position after traveling around the wheel. During a short observation, the patch passes the starting position four times. The observer began counting just after releasing it from that position, so the release itself is not a completed turn. The notebook therefore records four complete turns and keeps the starting moment separate from the later returns.

A class is preparing a display about light passing through openings. The display has a cardboard wall, two removable covers, and a lamp aimed at the wall. One cover has a narrow vertical opening; the other has a narrow horizontal opening. Only one cover is used at a time. Place a white sheet behind the wall before turning on the lamp. If the vertical cover is fitted, draw the bright shape on the left side of the record page. If the horizontal cover is fitted, draw it on the right. Write the cover name below each drawing. Keep the lamp and sheet in the same positions when changing covers. This allows visitors to compare the shapes while knowing that the opening changed and the distance between the lamp, wall, and sheet did not.

One cover has a narrow vertical opening; the other has a narrow horizontal opening. Only one cover is used at a time. Place a white sheet behind the wall before turning on the lamp. Keep the lamp and sheet in the same positions when changing covers. A hillside map uses a dotted border for exposed rock. Nila first reads that key, then finds a dotted patch above the footpath. A note beside the map gives its printing date. Another note names the mapmaker. Nila describes the patch as exposed rock, using the border key rather than either note about the map's production.

A note beside a hillside map gives its printing date. Another note names the mapmaker. The map uses a dotted border for exposed rock. Nila reads that key, then finds a dotted patch above the footpath. Nila describes the patch as exposed rock, using the border key rather than either note about the map's production.

Two photographs show the same sea arch from opposite sides. One was taken in bright sunshine; the other was taken under cloud. Both include a numbered scale pole beside the opening. To compare the opening's height, use the scale poles. The different sky colors describe the photographs' lighting but do not supply a height measurement.

Two photographs show the same sea arch from opposite sides. One was taken in bright sunshine; the other was taken under cloud. Both include a numbered scale pole beside the opening. To compare the lighting conditions, use the skies rather than the scale poles. The different sky colors describe the photographs' lighting but do not supply a height measurement.

An island guide divides the shore into numbered survey sections. Section seven includes a small inlet and the two headlands on either side. The inlet, which looks narrow from the hill but opens into a wider bay beyond the western headland, belongs to section seven. A visitor sees the wider water and assumes it must form a separate section. The guide explains that section numbers follow the drawn boundaries, not a visitor's impression of the shore's shape. The visitor checks the boundary before adding a new number to the sketch.

It looks narrow from the hill but opens into a wider bay beyond the western headland. A visitor sees the wider water and assumes it must form a separate section. The guide explains that section numbers follow the drawn boundaries, not a visitor's impression of the shore's shape. The visitor checks the boundary before adding a new number to the sketch.

For a playground weather survey, mark the observation place with a chalk circle. Take every reading from that circle so that moving between shade and sunlight does not change the location being compared. A wall notice describes yesterday's class meeting. A second notice describes next week's art display. A third notice lists the library opening times. After reading the notices, return to the survey record and write where today's reading was taken. Use the marked observation place, rather than the place where you happened to stand while reading the wall.

For a playground weather survey, mark the observation place with a chalk circle. Take every reading from that circle so that moving between shade and sunlight does not change the location being compared. A wall notice reminds pupils to use the chalk circle. A second notice repeats that location. A third notice again points to the same circle. After reading the notices, return to the survey record and write where today's reading was taken. Use the marked observation place, rather than the place where you happened to stand while reading the wall.

A relief model represents a valley with raised sides and a low center. The model is made from layers of card, and each layer represents the same increase in height. A steep slope crosses several layers in a short horizontal distance. A gentle slope crosses the same number of layers over a longer distance. The teacher calls the raised sides the valley walls and the low center the valley floor. Those names describe parts of the model, not separate pieces added afterward. A learner is asked to trace a route from one valley wall, across the valley floor, and up the other wall. Before tracing, the learner checks which labels name the raised sides and which label names the low center. The route must cross all three named parts, even where the cardboard pieces share one continuous surface.

A steep slope crosses several layers in a short horizontal distance. A gentle slope crosses the same number of layers over a longer distance. The teacher uses two pairs of equivalent names: raised sides or valley walls, and low center or valley floor. Those names describe parts of the model, not separate pieces added afterward. A class compares an open pine cone with a closed pine cone. Both came from the same tree. The open cone has spaces between its scales, while the closed cone has scales pressed together. Ella photographs the open cone beside a ruler. Her caption says that this specimen has separated scales; specimen refers to the photographed cone.

A class compares an open pine cone with a closed pine cone. Both came from the same tree. The open cone has spaces between its scales, while the closed cone has scales pressed together. Ella photographs the open cone beside a ruler. Her caption says that the photographed open cone has separated scales.

In a pond diagram, arrows show where food goes after one animal eats another. A tiny insect is eaten by a small fish. The fish is later eaten by a larger fish. The first arrow therefore points from the insect to the small fish. It describes food moving between animals, not the direction in which either animal swims.

In a pond diagram, arrows show where food goes after one animal eats another. A tiny insect is eaten by a small fish. The fish is later eaten by a larger fish. The first arrow must not point from the small fish to the insect. It describes food moving between animals, not the direction in which either animal swims.

A school nature club records holes in fallen leaves without collecting living plants. Choose one leaf that is already on the ground and place it on plain paper. Trace its outer edge, then mark each hole inside the outline. Count holes that are fully surrounded by leaf tissue separately from missing pieces along the edge. Write the date below the drawing. The record should let another pupil distinguish an internal hole from damage at the boundary, even if the actual leaf is no longer available when the drawings are compared.

A school nature club records holes in fallen leaves without collecting living plants. Choose one leaf that is already on the ground and place it on plain paper. Trace its outer edge, then mark each hole inside the outline. Count holes that are fully surrounded by leaf tissue separately from missing pieces along the edge. Write the date below the drawing and add an arrow showing which end held the leaf stalk. The record should let another pupil distinguish an internal hole from damage at the boundary, even if the actual leaf is no longer available when the drawings are compared.

A seed packet includes a drawing of a young bean plant. The first root points downward, while a curved shoot lifts the first leaves above it. In this drawing, the seed coat means the outer covering that surrounded the seed before growth began. Part of the seed coat still rests beside the new shoot. A pupil labels the root and shoot, then circles the remaining seed coat. The circle identifies the covering rather than the living shoot that has emerged from it. Each label refers to a different visible part.

At a garden observation table, pupils watch a harmless woodlouse move across a divided tray. One half contains damp paper and the other contains dry paper. The tray also has a shaded edge where the animal can leave the open area. The pupils agree to record a choice only when the animal's whole body has crossed the center line. If it pauses with its body across the line, they record an unfinished crossing. During the first observation, its front reaches the damp side while its back remains on the dry side. The recorder leaves the choice column empty and writes unfinished crossing in the notes. This record follows the agreed rule rather than guessing where the animal intended to go. After a brief observation, the pupils return it to the damp place where they found it.

At a garden observation table, pupils watch a harmless woodlouse move across a divided tray. One half contains damp paper and the other contains dry paper. The tray also has a shaded edge where the animal can leave the open area. The pupils agree to record a choice only when the animal's whole body has crossed the center line. Unless its whole body clears the line, they record an unfinished crossing, including a pause across the line. During the first observation, its front reaches the damp side while its back remains on the dry side. The recorder leaves the choice column empty and writes unfinished crossing in the notes. This record follows the agreed rule rather than guessing where the animal intended to go. After a brief observation, the pupils return it to the damp place where they found it.

A tile puzzle gives each star token a value of three. The board also shows decorative circles with no value. A player places two star tokens beside a blank total box. The puzzle title and page number appear below the board. To fill the box, the player adds the values of the two stars and writes six.

The board of a tile puzzle shows decorative circles with no value. A player places two star tokens beside a blank total box. The puzzle title and page number appear below the board. Each star token has a value of three. To fill the box, the player adds the values of the two stars and writes six.

A table lists each runner's starting number, finishing place, and shirt color. To find who finished second, read the finishing-place column. Starting numbers identify runners but do not rank their results. Shirt colors help match runners to photographs. Circle one row only after checking the column heading that matches the question being asked.

A table lists each runner's starting number, finishing place, and shirt color. To match a runner to a photograph, read the shirt-color column. Starting numbers identify runners but do not rank their results. Shirt colors help match runners to photographs. Circle one row only after checking the column heading that matches the question being asked.

A class draws rectangles on squared paper and counts the small squares inside them. The rectangle that has four rows, each containing six squares, covers twenty-four small squares. Counting the rows and multiplying by the number in each row gives the same answer as counting every square separately. A second rectangle is turned on its side. Its rows and columns exchange roles, but turning the paper does not add or remove any squares. The class uses this example to distinguish a change in orientation from a change in the amount of covered space.

Its rows and columns exchange roles, but turning the paper does not add or remove any squares. Ravi makes a tally mark whenever a visitor chooses the yellow badge. Five marks are grouped by drawing the fifth across the other four. Before counting the final groups, he reads three notes from the display team. One describes a new entrance banner. Another explains where spare pencils are kept. The last lists tomorrow's helpers. Ravi then returns to the tally and counts each complete group as five choices. The notes concern the display, but they do not change what a completed group of tally marks represents.

Ravi makes a tally mark whenever a visitor chooses the yellow badge. Five marks are grouped by drawing the fifth across the other four. Before counting the final groups, he reads three notes from the display team. One says that a completed tally group represents five choices. Another repeats that rule. The last reminds him of the same grouping rule. Ravi then returns to the tally and counts each complete group as five choices. The notes concern the display, but they do not change what a completed group of tally marks represents.

A game board shows a collection of counters in two different pictures. In the first picture, the counters are arranged in three separate clusters. Each cluster contains four counters. In the second picture, the same twelve counters stand in one long row. No counter has been added or removed between pictures. The teacher asks pupils to describe both the total and the arrangement. One pupil says that the first picture contains three groups of four. Another says that it shows four counters repeated in three clusters. Their words organize the description differently, but both identify the same arrangement. When the class compares the row with the clusters, it keeps the total separate from the way the counters are positioned. A drawing may therefore look different while still representing an equal number of objects.

A game board shows a collection of counters in two different pictures. In the first picture, the counters are arranged in three separate clusters. Each cluster contains four counters. In the second picture, the same twelve counters stand in one long row. No counter has been added or removed between pictures. The teacher asks pupils to describe both the total and the arrangement. One pupil says that the first picture contains three groups of four. Another says that it shows twelve counters divided into three equal clusters. Their words organize the description differently, but both identify the same arrangement. When the class compares the row with the clusters, it keeps the total separate from the way the counters are positioned. A drawing program saves a picture under the name Harbor. Lina makes a copy called Harbor draft before changing its colors. She opens the copy and adds a blue border. The original picture remains in a separate file. In her notes, the edited version means Harbor draft, so another pupil can open the file with the border.

The original picture remains in a separate file. In her notes, the edited version means Harbor draft, so another pupil can open the file with the border.

A classroom robot follows messages sent from a tablet. The tablet sends a turn instruction to the robot, and the robot sends a completion message back. These are two messages with opposite directions. A diagram should show who sends each message and who receives it, even though the same two devices take part in both exchanges.

A classroom robot follows messages sent from a tablet. The robot receives a turn instruction from the tablet, and the tablet receives a completion message from the robot. These are two messages with opposite directions. A diagram should show who sends each message and who receives it, even though the same two devices take part in both exchanges.

A teacher projects a spreadsheet containing a list of classroom books. Each row has a title, an author, and a shelf number. Amir sorts the list by title and sees the shelf numbers move with their books. He checks that each complete row stayed together during the sort. Otherwise a title might be paired with the shelf number of a different book. The printed copy on the desk still has the old order, so Amir compares complete records rather than expecting matching books to occupy the same row number in both versions.

A teacher projects a spreadsheet containing a list of classroom books. Each row has a title, an author, and a shelf number. Amir sorts the list by title and sees the shelf numbers move with their books. He checks that each complete row stayed together during the sort and that the heading row stayed at the top. Otherwise a title might be paired with the shelf number of a different book. The printed copy on the desk still has the old order, so Amir compares complete records rather than expecting matching books to occupy the same row number in both versions.

A school website offers two versions of a class photograph. One has many tiny colored squares, while the other uses fewer squares to show the same scene. A pixel is one of these tiny colored squares in a digital image. When the smaller version is enlarged, its pixels become easier to see. The pupils compare the two enlarged pictures and describe which edges look more blocky. They keep the displayed width equal so that a difference in enlargement size does not become another reason for the pictures to look different.

A simple animation uses three picture frames to show a paper boat moving across a pond. The first frame places the boat near the left bank, the second places it in the center, and the third places it near the right bank. The program normally displays the frames in that order. A practice rule says that pressing the return button displays the same frames in reverse order. The learner is asked what happens after the return button is pressed. If the return button has been pressed, begin with the right-bank picture and finish with the left-bank picture. The pictures themselves do not change; only their order changes. The learner writes the names of the first and last pictures to explain the result without needing to redraw all three frames or assume that the program creates a new picture.

A museum card says that a clay lamp was found in storage room four. The card also names the photographer and gives the date of the latest photograph. A visitor copies the discovery location onto a worksheet. The correct entry is storage room four; the place where an object was photographed is not stated on this card.

A museum card names the photographer of a clay lamp and gives the date of the latest photograph. It says that the lamp was found in storage room four. A visitor copies the discovery location onto a worksheet. The correct entry is storage room four; the place where an object was photographed is not stated on this card.

A family album contains a postcard with writing on both sides. The front names the coastal town shown in the picture. The back gives the sender's address in a different town. To identify the pictured place, Mara copies the name from the front. The address identifies where the sender could receive letters, not necessarily where the picture was taken.

A family album contains a postcard with writing on both sides. The front names the coastal town shown in the picture. The back gives the sender's address in a different town. To identify where letters could reach the sender, Mara copies the address from the back. The address identifies where the sender could receive letters, not necessarily where the picture was taken.

An archive keeps two copies of a market announcement. The copy that carries a handwritten correction beside the printed closing time belongs to the town clerk's collection. The other copy has no correction. A student compares them and records both the printed time and the later handwritten time. The student does not silently replace the first with the second, because the purpose is to describe how the document changed. The collection name helps identify which copy contains the added writing when the two sheets are displayed beside one another.

A local history box contains an undated invitation and a diary entry. The diary states that the hall opened on the morning of the invitation's event. A catalog page also describes the box's wooden lid, its replacement hinge, and the shelf where it was stored last winter. The student is trying to connect the invitation with the hall opening. The diary supplies that connection. Details about the box help identify its container, but they do not provide a second date for the event or change the link stated in the diary.

A local history box contains an undated invitation and a diary entry. The diary states that the hall opened on the morning of the invitation's event. A catalog page repeats that the hall opened on the morning of the event and points again to the same diary entry. The student is trying to connect the invitation with the hall opening. The diary supplies that connection. Details about the box help identify its container, but they do not provide a second date for the event or change the link stated in the diary.

A class is making an exhibit about an old printing workshop. Three labels describe a single wooden tool used to press paper against inked letters. The workshop inventory calls it the hand press. A later photograph caption calls it the wooden press. A repair note identifies it as the large press beside the window. Before making three exhibit entries, compare the identifying details on the labels. The inventory number is the same in all three records, and the repair note says that the tool was moved away from the window afterward. Create one exhibit entry for the tool and attach the three descriptions to it. Keep the movement note as part of its history. The change of position and the different descriptions should remain visible without turning one recorded object into three separate objects.

At a neighborhood repair fair, a volunteer gives each visitor a numbered card. The visitor keeps the card while the object being repaired receives a matching tag. Bea places a radio on the waiting shelf and holds card twelve. When a helper calls that number, Bea brings the card so the helper can match her to the tagged radio.

Bea places a radio on the waiting shelf and holds card twelve. When a helper calls twelve, Bea brings card twelve so the helper can match her to the tagged radio.

A school exchange board records borrowed sports equipment. One line says that Oak class lent a net to Elm class. A second line records Elm class returning the net to Oak class. The class names appear in both lines, but their roles change. Read the action as well as the names before deciding which class holds the net.

A school exchange board records borrowed sports equipment. One line says that Elm class lent a net to Oak class. A second line records Oak class returning the net to Elm class. The class names appear in both lines, but their roles change. Read the action as well as the names before deciding which class holds the net.

A community room offers two rehearsal periods on Saturday. The early period ends before the caretaker's lunch break, and the later period begins afterward. A puppet group needs one uninterrupted period long enough for its show. The organizer compares the show length with the length of each period. Combining unused minutes from opposite sides of the lunch break would not provide an uninterrupted rehearsal. The organizer therefore checks each period separately and writes down the one that can contain the complete show from its beginning to its end.

A community room offers two rehearsal periods on Saturday. The early period ends before the caretaker's lunch break, and the later period begins afterward. A puppet group needs one uninterrupted period long enough for its show. The organizer compares the show length with the length of each period and checks whether the puppet screen is available then. Combining unused minutes from opposite sides of the lunch break would not provide an uninterrupted rehearsal. The organizer therefore checks each period separately and writes down the one that can contain the complete show from its beginning to its end.

A classroom meeting uses a talking token so that pupils can hear one speaker at a time. The holder is the person currently carrying the token. Place the token in the center when nobody is speaking. Before beginning a comment, pick it up and wait until the room is quiet. The holder returns it to the center after finishing. Another pupil may then take it. Record the order of speakers by name, rather than numbering their seats, because pupils may move between seats while the meeting continues.

A classroom meeting uses a talking token so that pupils can hear one speaker at a time. Place the token in the center when nobody is speaking. The holder is the person currently carrying the token. Before beginning a comment, pick it up and wait until the room is quiet. The holder returns it to the center after finishing. Another pupil may then take it. Record the order of speakers by name, rather than numbering their seats, because pupils may move between seats while the meeting continues.

A neighborhood book exchange has a shelf for books that are ready to borrow and a tray for books waiting to be checked. A book goes onto the borrowing shelf only after a volunteer has confirmed that all its pages are present. A colored slip inside the cover records that check. If the slip is missing, the book stays in the checking tray. This rule applies even when the cover looks new and the title is already listed in the exchange notebook. The notebook records which titles people have offered, while the slip records whether a particular copy has been checked. A volunteer finds two copies of the same story, one with a slip and one without. Their matching titles do not allow the volunteer to treat the unchecked copy as though it already carries the other copy's slip.

A neighborhood book exchange has a shelf for books that are ready to borrow and a tray for books waiting to be checked. A book goes onto the borrowing shelf only after a volunteer has confirmed that all its pages are present. A colored slip inside the cover records that check. If the slip is present, the book may leave the checking tray for the borrowing shelf. This rule applies even when the cover looks new and the title is already listed in the exchange notebook. In a short play, the name Lantern refers to a person, not a light. The script lists a garden bench and an empty basket as scenery. A stage note describes the evening sky. Later, Lantern enters carrying a letter. A reader who recalls the character list will understand that a person enters; the scene does not suddenly introduce a walking lamp.

A short play lists a garden bench and an empty basket as scenery. A stage note describes the evening sky. The name Lantern refers to a person, not a light. Later, Lantern enters carrying a letter. A reader who recalls the character list will understand that a person enters; the scene does not suddenly introduce a walking lamp.

A story says that Noor hides a silver button in a flour jar before leaving the kitchen. Later, her brother searches a blue tin for the missing button. To identify where the button actually is, use Noor's action. The brother's search tells us what he suspects, but the passage does not say that he has found or moved it.

A story says that Noor hides a silver button in a flour jar before leaving the kitchen. Later, her brother searches a blue tin for the missing button. To identify where the brother thinks the button might be, use his search. The brother's search tells us what he suspects, but the passage does not say that he has found or moved it.

An editing exercise asks pupils to make a long sentence easier to follow without changing its events. Read the sentence about the messenger, who crossed the crowded courtyard while the musicians were rehearsing beside the gate, arriving at the tower. First identify who arrived and where the arrival happened. Then place the courtyard crossing in a separate sentence if that makes the sequence clearer. Keep the musicians beside the gate; they are part of the background, not the people who arrive at the tower. Compare the revised version with every event in the original.

An editing exercise asks pupils to make a long sentence easier to follow without changing its events. Read these events: the messenger crossed the crowded courtyard and arrived at the tower; meanwhile, musicians rehearsed beside the gate. First identify who arrived and where the arrival happened. Then place the courtyard crossing in a separate sentence if that makes the sequence clearer. Keep the musicians beside the gate; they are part of the background, not the people who arrive at the tower. Compare the revised version with every event in the original.

In a folktale exercise, a red ribbon marks the door that the traveler must use on returning. The next paragraph describes a painted ceiling, a cracked floor tile, and a row of shoes under a bench. None of these details changes the door marker. At the end of the exercise, the reader is asked which door the traveler should choose. The answer must come from the ribbon rule introduced earlier. Attractive descriptions may enrich a story while remaining separate from the particular detail needed to follow a character's plan.

In a folktale exercise, a red ribbon marks the door that the traveler must use on returning. The next paragraph describes the red ribbon again, repeats its color, and reminds the reader that it marks the returning traveler's door. None of these details changes the door marker. At the end of the exercise, the reader is asked which door the traveler should choose. The answer must come from the ribbon rule introduced earlier. Attractive descriptions may enrich a story while remaining separate from the particular detail needed to follow a character's plan.

During a reading workshop, Tessa notices that a story uses several descriptions for its main traveler. The opening calls her the map seller. A later paragraph calls her the woman with the rolled maps. Near the end, a child addresses her as Aunt Suri. The story explains that the child is her nephew and that she carries the same bundle of maps throughout the journey. Tessa first writes three names in her character list, then draws lines between them after checking these clues. She combines the entries into one character record and keeps each description beside it. This lets her remember how different people recognize the traveler without adding extra travelers to the story. A percussion score gives a hollow circle to a soft drum tap and a filled circle to a loud tap. The opening pattern has a hollow circle followed by two filled circles. A pupil points to the first symbol and calls it the quiet one. That description refers to the soft tap, not to either of the later loud taps.

For a shadow performance, one pupil moves a paper bird between a lamp and a screen. Another pupil watches from the opposite side of the screen. Ask the mover to tilt the bird while the watcher describes its shadow. The person giving the description should report the visible shape, while the other person controls the paper figure.

A gallery activity asks visitors to compare two prints made from the same carved block. One print uses dark ink on pale paper. The other uses pale ink on dark paper. Because the carved block is unchanged, its lines and empty areas occur in corresponding places in both prints. To compare the effect of reversing the colors, display the prints at equal sizes. Enlarging only one would make its lines appear thicker as well. The activity separates the effect of the color choice from the effect of changing the picture's scale.

The activity separates the effect of the color choice from the effect of changing the picture's scale.

A student composes a short tune for a classroom instrument. The tune begins with three notes that return near the end. A motif is a short musical idea that can appear more than once in a piece. The student circles the returning motif on the score and draws a line back to its first appearance. One note in the return is held longer, but the student can still recognize the three-note pattern. The annotation records both the repeated idea and the changed length of one sound.

A school exhibition includes two woven paper mats. Both use strips of the same width, but their makers chose different color sequences. The first mat repeats blue, blue, yellow across its width. The second alternates blue and yellow. A display note asks visitors to identify a complete repeat before counting how many repeats fit across a mat. If a sequence ends before its last required color, do not count that unfinished part as a complete repeat. The first mat has an extra blue strip at one edge after several complete groups. That strip still belongs to the mat, even though it does not complete another blue, blue, yellow group. The comparison therefore distinguishes the number of visible strips from the number of complete repeating groups. Visitors can describe both quantities without pretending that the extra strip has disappeared.

A flat-pack display stand marks its back panel with a triangle. The instruction sheet also lists the package weight and the name of the designer. Before attaching the small ledge, find the back panel and lay it flat. Use the triangle to identify it; the weight and designer's name do not distinguish one panel from another.

A reusable lunch box has a removable divider and a sliding name window. The divider separates foods, while the window holds a card identifying the owner. To stop two foods from touching, adjust the divider. Changing the name card serves a different purpose and does not alter the arrangement of food inside the box.

A design class examines a folding stool without sitting on it. The support bar that connects the two rear legs beneath the fabric seat stops those legs from spreading farther apart. Lin points to the bar and traces its connection to each leg. She then draws the fabric seat separately so that its surface does not hide the support in her sketch. The teacher asks her to label the part that limits the distance between the rear legs, rather than simply labeling the largest visible surface of the stool.

Two pencil cases close in different ways. One uses a zipper, and the other uses a flap that tucks into a loop. The task is to compare how each case keeps pencils inside when it is closed. A product card also describes the zipper case's printed stars, the flap case's striped lining, and the color of each carrying handle. After reading the card, a pupil explains the closing methods. The decorative details identify the cases but are not additional mechanisms holding either opening shut.

A classroom organizer has a shallow removable tray inside a larger storage box. The maker's drawing labels the removable part as the sorting tray. A note on the side calls it the top insert, and the packing list calls it the shallow compartment. The instructions explain that these three names refer to the same removable part. A pupil preparing the organizer initially expects to find three small pieces in the package. She compares the drawing with the packing list and notices that there is only one matching outline. She places the tray inside the box and writes the three names beside a single sketch. The larger box remains a separate item because it surrounds the tray and can be used after the tray is lifted out. Different descriptions therefore need to be matched to objects before the parts can be counted.
